So, I realize this is probably an unpopular opinion - most atheists love the Satanic Temple and the things they do. I actually didn't mind them for a long time either, until I started putting some thought into it. Lately the Satanic Temple and Satanism in general have been growing in popularity and gathering support in their fight against symbols of religion in government. Now, while I still agree with the message, I have to disagree with the methods. I hope to explain why here, as well as to get some insight from other atheists, and hopefully start a discussion.

1) The Satanic Temple represents a religion

As an anti-theist as well as an atheist, I oppose religion. This means that I am against the notion of Satanism as a religion, even if it's fairly benign when compared to other religions. In my opinion, religion does nothing but needlessly complicate society. Satanism is a religion, and its primary goal seems to be to promote secularism by using Satanic imagery to foster "religious equality" in government. I don't particularly want religious equality in government - I don't want religion in government at all.

2) The Satanic Temple antagonizes the religious

Although I am an anti-theist, I do not advocate for the antagonization of the religious. Most of us atheists were religious at one time in our lives, whether dogmatically or just because our parents raised us that way. In my opinion, it is far better to open an honest and polite dialogue with the religious than to purposely antagonize them. While the form of "activism" that the Satanic Temple practices can be effective in the short term, it also results in lots of vitriol from both sides, which is unproductive to their overall goal. Further, it doesn't appear to teach anyone anything, other than the idea that fighting fire with fire is a good solution to a problem.

3) The Satanic Temple targets Christianity and Catholocism specifically

While Christianity and Catholicism represent large portions of the religious population, especially in America, they are far from the only religions, and are definitely not the only religions which cause problems. In my opinion, it is better to address the idea that religion as a whole is bad for a peaceful society, rather than target specific religions and treat them as if they are special.

4) The Satanic Temple validates Christianity / Catholicism

Building on the point above, the Satanic Temple's imagery and overall theme treat Christianity as if it's special, and give weight to it by appropriating aspects of it. As atheists, we accept the fact that there is no reason to believe that anything supernatural is real. While the Satanic Temple claims to believe in a "literary" Satan as opposed to a literal Satan, it still gives validation to the concept of Satan as a figure. In reality, there is no reason to think that Satan as a character is any more compelling to or in reality than, say, Voldemort.

5) There's no real reason to use Satanism to combat religion

At its heart, Satanism as a method to combat religion is just a bully tactic. The arguments against the supernatural are sound enough to stand on their own legs - we don't need to resort to what is essentially name-calling in order to make ourselves heard or affect change in the world. Since, I think, most members of the Satanic Temple would self-identify as atheists anyway, there's simply no need to operate under the guise of a religion in order to get things done. Further, there are plenty of great atheist organizations out there which are already doing their part to oppose the same things as the Satanic Temple, and in most cases are doing a great job of it.

So, what should we do about it?

Honestly, probably nothing. No one can argue with the fact that they're getting things done and causing some discussion. They'll most likely continue to build steam, and actively opposing them would probably just further divide a community which should be banding together. However, this doesn't mean we shouldn't talk about it. All movements need discussion in order to grow and prosper, and the same can be said for the secular movement.
